overview: Giganotosaurus carolinii was a carcharodontosaurid theropod from the Cenomanian of Patagonia (~98 Ma), and with an estimated length of 12–13 metres it is among the longest carnivorous dinosaurs ever found. Discovered by amateur fossil hunter Rubén Carolini in 1993 in the Neuquén Group, it briefly held the title of "largest carnivore ever" before overlapping size estimates with Spinosaurus and Tyrannosaurus complicated the comparison.

As a carcharodontosaurid, Giganotosaurus was more closely related to Carcharodontosaurus of North Africa than to Tyrannosaurus — yet the two giants lived at almost the same time, representing parallel evolution of enormous predators on separate landmasses. Giganotosaurus shared its ecosystem with the titanosaur Argentinosaurus.

fossilSites.name: Candeleros Formation
fossilSites.note: Cenomanian fluvial and aeolian deposits with the Giganotosaurus type specimen and the giant titanosaur Argentinosaurus in the same unit.

articles.title: Discovery
articles.body: Rubén Carolini spotted the bones eroding from a hillside in the Neuquén badlands in 1993. Coria and Salgado described Giganotosaurus carolinii in 1995, naming the species for its discoverer. The skull, much of the postcranium and several fragmentary additional specimens are now known. A related genus, Mapusaurus, is known from a multi-individual bonebed in the same region, potentially suggesting group behaviour in carcharodontosaurids.

articles.title: Size comparison
articles.body: Giganotosaurus skull length (~1.8 m) rivals or exceeds Tyrannosaurus. Body length estimates range from 12–13.5 m, comparable to Tyrannosaurus but with a more slender build and proportionally lower body mass (~6–8 tonnes versus ~8–14 tonnes for large T. rex). The comparison is complicated by incomplete material for both, but Giganotosaurus was unquestionably among the very largest terrestrial carnivores.

articles.title: Predatory role
articles.body: The co-occurrence with the titanosaur Argentinosaurus — potentially the heaviest land animal ever — in the Candeleros Formation has led to suggestions that Giganotosaurus hunted these giants. The carcharodontosaurid skull, with blade-like serrated teeth and a wide gape, would have been effective for inflicting large wounds and blood loss rather than bone-crushing bites. Group behaviour in the related Mapusaurus (multi-individual bonebed) suggests possible cooperative hunting in the lineage.

fossilRecord.evidence: Large skull bones and serrated teeth support its identity as one of the largest known theropods.

record.mya: early Cenomanian, roughly 99-97 million years ago
record.description: Giganotosaurus carolinii was a giant carcharodontosaurid predator from the Candeleros Formation of Patagonia. It is known from one incomplete skeleton with much of the skull and a referred partial lower jaw; no complete skeleton exists.
facts: Its skull is reconstructed from incomplete and distorted bones.
It rivalled the largest theropods in length, but claims that it was definitively larger than Tyrannosaurus depend on uncertain reconstructions and mass models.
Blade-like serrated teeth support predation on large vertebrates; specific prey and hunting groups are unknown.

animalParagraphs: Giganotosaurus was a huge theropod from the early Late Cretaceous of Patagonia. Length estimates of roughly 12–13 metres and mass estimates from about four to eight tonnes come from an incomplete skeleton and depend on how the missing parts are reconstructed, so comparisons with Tyrannosaurus and Spinosaurus are not settled.

Its skull was long and low with blade-like, serrated teeth suited to slicing flesh rather than crushing bone, and its braincase was small relative to body size. The skull bones are incomplete and distorted, so the published skull length of around 1.5–1.8 metres is a reconstruction.

It lived alongside giant titanosaurian sauropods such as Andesaurus and rebbachisaurids, and large sauropods are usually assumed to have been among its prey. Whether it hunted alone or in groups is unknown; the related Mapusaurus has been found in a multi-individual bonebed, but no such evidence exists for Giganotosaurus.
animalHighlights: Among the largest theropods known, though its exact size relative to Tyrannosaurus depends on reconstruction.
Blade-like teeth and a long, low skull mark it as a carcharodontosaurid rather than a tyrannosaur-like bone-crusher.
Discovered by an amateur fossil hunter, Rubén Carolini, whose name the species carries.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.reason: Serrated, laterally compressed teeth indicate slicing flesh from large prey; specific prey species are not documented by bite marks or gut contents.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Robust hindlimbs and small forelimbs indicate two-legged walking; speed estimates are model-based and vary widely.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: The holotype is described as about 70 per cent complete; length and mass rely on reconstructing missing regions, and a second jaw suggests slightly larger individuals existed.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: Body proportions are reasonably constrained; the distorted skull, skin texture and colour are not directly known.

whereFacts.label: Type locality
whereFacts.value: Near Villa El Chocón, Neuquén Province, Argentina

locality.name: Villa El Chocón
locality.note: Candeleros Formation badlands south of the Ezequiel Ramos Mexía reservoir. The skeleton is housed in the local Museo Municipal Ernesto Bachmann.

presentation.classificationSummary: Giganotosaurus is a carcharodontosaurine carcharodontosaurid, a member of the giant allosauroid radiation that dominated Gondwanan faunas in the mid-Cretaceous. It is closely related to Mapusaurus from slightly younger Argentine rocks and to Carcharodontosaurus from North Africa.

related.reason: A close relative from the overlying Huincul Formation known from a multi-individual bonebed.
Compare with the African carcharodontosaurid that gives the family its name.
Compare with the North American giant it is most often measured against.

questions.title: How heavy was it?
questions.copy: Estimates range from about four to over eight tonnes depending on the model and on how the incomplete skeleton is reconstructed.

questions.title: What did the complete skull look like?
questions.copy: The preserved skull bones are incomplete and distorted, so total skull length and snout shape are reconstructed rather than measured.

questions.title: Did it hunt sauropods in groups?
questions.copy: Giant sauropods shared its habitat, but no bite marks, trackways or bonebeds document either its prey or any group behaviour.

evidence.confidenceLimit: High for giant size and carcharodontosaurid identity; moderate for proportions; low for exact mass and behaviour.

specimens.name: Holotype
specimens.institution: Museo Municipal Ernesto Bachmann, Villa El Chocón
specimens.note: Incomplete skeleton with much of the skull, braincase, vertebrae, pelvis and hindlimbs; estimated at about 70 per cent complete by its describers.

specimens.name: Referred dentary
specimens.institution: Museo de Geología y Paleontología, Universidad Nacional del Comahue
specimens.note: Partial lower jaw about eight per cent larger than the holotype, referred by Calvo and Coria in 1998.

panel.headline: One substantial skeleton and a second lower jaw.
panel.standfirst: Giganotosaurus rests on a single incomplete skeleton with much of the skull, pelvis and limbs, plus a referred partial dentary from a slightly larger animal. Its giant size is secure; its precise proportions are not.

coverage.label: Moderate
coverage.basis: Most skeletal regions are represented in the holotype, but from one individual, with an incomplete and distorted skull and missing forelimb and tail elements.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: The holotype includes much of the skull and lower jaws, the braincase, most of the vertebral column, ribs, the pelvis and the hindlimbs, and was estimated by its describers at about 70 per cent complete. A separate partial dentary about eight per cent larger was later referred to the genus.
knownRemains.note: Because a single individual supplies almost all the anatomy, size estimates and skull proportions carry more uncertainty than the animal's fame suggests.

media.title: Original skull bones of the holotype

media.caption: Original bones from the right side of the holotype skull on display at Villa El Chocón. The mounted skeleton nearby is a cast with the missing regions reconstructed.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: Much of the skull including maxillae, lower jaws with teeth and a well-preserved braincase; bones are incomplete and distorted, so total skull length is reconstructed.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Most of the neck, back and sacrum with part of the tail and ribs; the tail end is missing.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Pelvis and hindlimbs including femur and tibia; the forelimbs are poorly represented.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: None. No skin, feathers, gut contents or bite-marked prey are known.

specimenCards.title: MUCPv-Ch1 · holotype
specimenCards.description: An incomplete skeleton found by Rubén Carolini in 1993 in the Candeleros Formation and described by Rodolfo Coria and Leonardo Salgado in 1995. It includes skull, braincase, vertebrae, pelvis and hindlimb bones.

specimenCards.title: MUCPv-95 · partial dentary
specimenCards.description: A fragment of lower jaw about eight per cent larger than the holotype's, described in 1998 and taken to show that Giganotosaurus reached somewhat larger sizes than the type individual.
specimenCards.meta: Candeleros Formation · Neuquén · Museo de la Universidad Nacional del Comahue

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: A single partial skeleton with much of the skull, plus a larger isolated dentary, both from the Candeleros Formation.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: A giant carcharodontosaurid predator of large prey, roughly comparable in length to Tyrannosaurus though with a lighter skull build; size rankings depend on reconstruction.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: Body mass, complete skull shape, forelimb and tail anatomy, growth, hunting behaviour and prey.
